title: The Sealed Nectar
author: Safiur Rahman Mubarakpuri
review: A biography of the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) that brings individual events into a connected life story. Reading in sequence helps keep each chapter in its wider context.

title: Wings of Fire
author: APJ Abdul Kalam
review: Kalam's journey from humble beginnings to a career in science gives persistence a concrete shape. A reminder that a large ambition is built through years of learning and work.

title: Steve Jobs
author: Walter Isaacson
review: A portrait of creative ambition and demanding leadership, with the difficult relationships left in view. The product story is inseparable from the way people worked together.

title: Elon Musk (Isaacson)
author: Walter Isaacson
review: A more complex portrait of Musk, with ambition and personal contradictions sharing the page. It invites a closer look at both what gets built and the pressures surrounding it.

title: Einstein: His Life and Universe
author: Walter Isaacson
review: Physics placed alongside the life of the person doing the thinking. The biographical perspective makes scientific ideas feel like questions someone had to struggle with before reaching an answer.

title: Code
author: Charles Petzold
review: From flashlights to CPUs, complex machinery becomes a sequence of understandable steps. A useful way to rebuild intuition about what sits underneath the software we write.

title: The Making of Prince of Persia
author: Jordan Mechner
review: A game developer's journal that lets the making of a game unfold day by day. The value is in seeing the work in progress, before it becomes a polished story about a finished creation.

title: Do You Remember Kunan Poshpora?
author: Zubaan
review: An account of violence and impunity that keeps attention on the people affected. Difficult reading that asks what it means to remember and to seek accountability.

title: Enjoy Your Life
author: Dr. Muhammad Al-Arifi
review: Practical reflections on human relationships and the way we treat one another. Small choices in conversation and everyday conduct deserve as much attention as our intentions.

title: Gems and Jewels
author: Abdul Malik Mujahid
review: Short stories that leave room to pause over a lesson before moving on. A book suited to reading a little at a time and carrying a question into the rest of the day.

title: When the Heavens Went on Sale
author: Ashlee Vance
review: The new space race viewed through the people trying to build their place in it. The appeal is seeing a vast ambition take shape through individual ventures and decisions.

title: Elon Musk (Vance)
author: Ashlee Vance
review: A view of the early Tesla and SpaceX years, when the eventual outcome was far less certain. The chaos gives context to the distance between a company's ambition and its ability to deliver.

title: Zero to One
author: Peter Thiel
review: An argument for building something distinct enough to escape direct competition. A useful question for a new product: what can it offer that another company cannot easily copy?

title: The Worlds I See
author: Fei-Fei Li
review: Fei-Fei Li's life story alongside her work in AI and computer vision. It brings a human perspective to a field often described through models and technical milestones.

title: How to Stop Worrying and Start Living
author: Dale Carnegie
review: Practical reflections on worry and the attention it takes from everyday life. A useful prompt to separate the problem in front of you from everything you imagine might follow.

title: Project Hail Mary
author: Andy Weir
review: Science fiction that makes working through a difficult problem part of the adventure. Curiosity and experimentation carry a story with room for both humour and feeling.

title: Guarding the Tongue
author: Imam al-Nawawi
review: A guide to mindful speech and the responsibility that comes with words. It makes the pause before speaking feel like an action worth practising in its own right.

title: User Friendly
author: Cliff Kuang
review: A reminder that interface choices shape what people understand and do. Useful for looking beyond how a product appears to the behaviour its design encourages.

title: The Design of Everyday Things
author: Don Norman
review: Even a door can reveal a mismatch between a design and the person using it. A foundation for asking whether an interface explains itself and makes the next action clear.

title: Atomic Habits
author: James Clear
review: A systems approach to improvement through small, repeatable changes. The useful shift is from wanting a result to arranging daily life so that the next good action is easier.

title: Calvin and Hobbes
author: Bill Watterson
review: Childhood imagination given room to take ordinary life somewhere unexpected. The humour is a reminder of how much there is to notice when familiar things are still open to question.
